quiz.title: Chapter 2 Quiz: Legal Research Platforms
quiz.intro: Ten questions on reading citations, retrieving known sources, and the mechanics of searching.

items.q: Before running any search, the chapter says the single most time-saving step is to:
options: Choose natural language over Boolean
Set the jurisdiction and source-type filters
Brainstorm synonyms
Run a citator check
items.why: A search for “reasonable accommodation” across all jurisdictions and source types buries you; filters keep irrelevant results out of the way (Understanding the Common Features).

items.q: In the citation Robles v. Domino’s Pizza, LLC, 913 F.3d 898 (9th Cir. 2019), what do “913” and “F.3d” tell you?
options: The docket number and the court
The volume and the reporter where the opinion is published
The page and the year
The circuit and the panel
items.why: A case citation reads Party v. Party, Volume Reporter Page (Court Year). The court and year in the parenthetical tell you how much authority the case may carry (Reading a Legal Citation).

items.q: You already have the citation 42 U.S.C. § 12182. The chapter says you should:
options: Search the party names to find it
Enter only the location parts (title and section) into the search bar and retrieve it
Run a natural language search describing the ADA
Search for the year of enactment
items.why: Retrieve, don’t search. The location portions are what the database indexes; names and years can interfere with a clean retrieval (Finding the Cited Source).

items.q: Natural language searching is the better starting point when:
options: You need to be sure you find every relevant document
You know the exact legal terminology
You are still exploring and do not yet know the precise terms of art
You are updating a case
items.why: Natural language tolerates ordinary language and ranks by closeness; Boolean is the tool once you know what you are after (Searching for Authorities).

items.q: Which search requires both a separation concept and a disability concept to appear in the document?
options: fired OR terminated OR disab!
(fired OR terminated OR discharged) AND (disab! OR “medical condition”)
fired NOT disab!
“fired terminated discharged”
items.why: OR gathers the variants of one concept; AND requires distinct concepts to co-occur (Practical Search Strategy).

items.q: The root expander bit! would retrieve which of the following?
options: Only bite and bites
bite, bitten, biting, and also bitter and bitcoin
Only words that end in “bit”
Nothing; the expander needs at least four letters
items.why: A short root drags in words you did not intend. Reach for the longest, most distinctive root that still captures the variants you need (Expansion Operators; Common Pitfalls).

items.q: The single-character wildcard wom*n is useful because it:
options: Retrieves every word beginning with wom
Fills exactly one character position, catching woman and women
Excludes the word women
Works only in Lexis
items.why: The asterisk fills one position; the root expander (!) handles variable endings (Expansion Operators).

items.q: The chapter’s caution about NOT is that it:
options: Is unavailable on most platforms
Can quietly delete good results when the excluded word sometimes travels with the authority you want
Must always be used with proximity connectors
Only works in natural language mode
items.why: Excluding a word is a blunt instrument; use it with restraint (Common Pitfalls).

items.q: As your questions move from exploratory to focusing to application, your searches should:
options: Stay as broad as possible to avoid missing anything
Narrow to match, adding precision tools like proximity connectors and ATLEAST
Switch from Boolean to natural language
Drop the jurisdiction filter
items.why: The progression of your searches should track the progression of your questions; Chapter 9 supplies the precision toolkit (Practical Search Strategy).

items.q: Which features does the chapter say are common across platforms and stable over time?
options: A central search box, jurisdiction and source-type filters, a citator, and a topical classification system
Identical button placement on every platform
Free access to all primary sources
Generative AI summaries
items.why: Learn the underlying concepts rather than the location of a button and your skills survive the next redesign (Understanding the Common Features).
